transcript:
Meeting: Photon Health x Redwood — Private deployment compliance deep dive (retention, audit logs, report pack)
Recorded: 2025-02-18 14:03:22 (America/Los_Angeles)
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees (Redwood): Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Kevin Osei (Eng — audit export/retention), Vivek Kulkarni (Private deployments), Marcus Lin (Security Eng)
Attendees (Photon Health): Erin Wallace (Security Eng), Miguel Santos (Platform Lead), Priya Desai (GRC), Hannah Cho (Infra)

Auto Summary (Fireflies):
- Photon asked for clarity on where logs live in Private and whether Redwood ever stores prompts/completions.
- Redwood explained retention policy evaluation happens in the control plane service; enforcement is via data plane purge jobs in the customer environment.
- Discussion covered TTL semantics, deletion verification metrics, and exception/hold workflows.
- Redwood walked through the baseline compliance reporting pack sections and how it will be generated/exported.

Questions captured:
- Can Photon set different TTLs per region and per data class?
- What happens if purge jobs fall behind (maintenance window, backlog)?
- How are audit logs protected from tampering and can they be sent to Photon’s SIEM?
- How is “no logging” handled vs “short retention”?


[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Alright, I think we’re recording. Um, thanks everybody for joining. This is the Photon Health private deployment compliance deep dive. Goal today is to get really concrete on where data lives, especially logs, and then how retention is enforced, and then what the compliance reporting pack looks like as an artifact that your auditors can accept.

[00:19] Markus Klein: Quick intros on our side: I’m Markus, solutions engineering. Kevin is here, he’s been building a lot of the audit export bits. Vivek is our private deployment stakeholder, like installer and defaults. And Marcus Lin, security engineering.

[00:31] Erin Wallace: Great, thanks. Erin, security engineering. Miguel from platform. Priya from compliance. Hannah from infra.

[00:40] Markus Klein: Awesome. Erin, do you want to set context, like what you need to be able to answer from your side?

[00:46] Erin Wallace: Yeah. We’re pushing toward a private deployment because of our data restrictions. So the biggest questions we keep getting internally are: where do request logs live, where do audit logs live, whether prompts or completions ever get persisted, and then if we set a retention like 30 days, how do we know it actually deletes. And then, we also need something we can hand to auditors, like a standardized report.

[01:09] Priya Desai: And I’ll add, like, we don’t need a custom GRC integration on day one, but we do need consistent evidence. Like, same report every quarter, the fields don’t change randomly.

[01:20] Markus Klein: Perfect. That aligns with the retention controls and the compliance reporting pack we’ve been building. Let’s start with deployment boundaries because that drives “where logs live.” Vivek, do you want to do the 2-minute private architecture?

[01:33] Vivek Kulkarni: Sure. So Redwood Private, in your case, would run in your VPC. It’s basically a customer-managed data plane: inference gateway, model runtime, and the associated telemetry pipeline components. The control plane can be either “private control plane” in the same environment or a constrained management plane depending on the package, but the core point is: the data stores for logs and telemetry are in your account. Redwood doesn’t get your prompts unless you explicitly export to us, which you wouldn’t.

[01:59] Miguel Santos: When you say “data stores,” do you mean like an S3 bucket in our AWS? Or can it be our existing Elasticsearch?

[02:06] Vivek Kulkarni: Exactly. Typical patterns: object storage for raw request logs, an indexed store like OpenSearch/Elastic for searchable logs if you want, and a metrics backend like Prometheus/Thanos, and tracing like Tempo/Jaeger, depending on your stack. Our installer supports a default bundle, but it’s configurable.

[02:25] Hannah Cho: Ok. So Redwood doesn’t run a SaaS collector that ships logs out, right?

[02:31] Vivek Kulkarni: By default, no. For private, telemetry stays in-cluster. You can optionally forward metrics to your centralized observability, but that’s within your environment.

[02:41] Markus Klein: Kevin, maybe define the data classes we’re talking about because I think “logs” gets overloaded.

[02:47] Kevin Osei: Yeah. We’ve been splitting it into a handful of data classes for retention purposes. One is request/response logs—think API gateway access logs plus application logs around inference requests. Another is prompts/completions content, which may be included inside request logs if you enable “payload logging,” but in private we strongly recommend disabled by default.

[03:09] Kevin Osei: Another is audit logs—those are separate and are security events: policy changes, user logins, role changes, API key creation, report exports, retention config changes, that kind of stuff. Then traces/metrics are separate. And then artifacts: like eval datasets or prompt sets if you upload them into the console, which in private can also be stored in your object storage.

[03:34] Erin Wallace: That’s helpful. So prompts/completions are not inherently stored unless we choose to log them?

[03:39] Kevin Osei: Correct. In most setups, your inference request body is transient. If you enable request logging, you can configure whether it includes full payload, headers only, or redacted. Retention controls apply to whichever stores are enabled.

[03:54] Priya Desai: Wait—so if we disable payload logging, we still have to retain something for audit? Like, for incident response you need something.

[04:03] Marcus Lin: Great question. Audit logs are not the same as request payload logs. Audit logs are usually required for compliance, and they don’t contain prompt text. They contain “who did what when” in the platform: “Erin changed retention policy from 90 days to 30 days,” “Miguel created a token,” “system exported audit logs,” etc.

[04:24] Marcus Lin: For incident response, you can have request metadata logs—timestamps, model ID, latency, error codes—without storing PHI. That’s a recommended pattern.

[04:35] Miguel Santos: So do you have a concept of “no logging mode” entirely? Or does the system force some minimum logs?

[04:42] Kevin Osei: For private, you can set request logging to minimal. There’s still some operational logs in the cluster because software runs, but the configurable “request/response log store” can be disabled. Audit logs we recommend always on. There are also minimums on audit log retention depending on your policy, but in private you control that.

[04:59] Erin Wallace: Ok, let’s talk retention enforcement. If we say request logs 14 days, audit logs 1 year, metrics 30 days, how is that evaluated and how is deletion done?

[05:11] Kevin Osei: The architecture is: a retention policy service stores your configured TTLs by data class. That policy is evaluated centrally (control plane logic), and the result is used by data plane purge jobs. So the purge jobs run on a schedule, they query the backing store for records older than now minus TTL, and delete in batches.

[05:33] Hannah Cho: Are those TTLs like database TTL indexes or are you doing explicit deletes?

[05:39] Kevin Osei: Depends on the store. For some stores we can use native TTL / lifecycle policies (e.g., object storage lifecycle rules), but for others, it’s explicit deletes. We have a generic purge job framework that’s idempotent and rate-limited.

[05:56] Miguel Santos: When you say “idempotent,” can you explain? Like if it runs twice, it won’t delete too much?

[06:03] Kevin Osei: Yeah. It uses a cutoff timestamp and a paging cursor. If it retries, it re-queries for “older than cutoff” and deletes what’s there. If already deleted, it’s a no-op. Also we cap batch sizes and have safety limits to avoid hammering your DB.

[06:19] Erin Wallace: How do we prove it’s doing what it says? Like, for auditors and also for us.

[06:25] Caleb Johnson (noted by Fireflies as Speaker 6): Uh sorry, I’m not on the invite, but I might’ve joined from the wrong link—

[06:30] Markus Klein: I think that’s a mis-join. No worries.

[06:33] Kevin Osei: Verification is via metrics. We emit TTL lag metrics per store: basically “oldest record age” vs expected. There’s a metric like ttl_lag_seconds by data class. We also emit purge_rows_deleted and purge_failures. Those go to dashboards.

[06:53] Hannah Cho: Is that per tenant? Because we don’t want cardinality explosion.

[06:57] Kevin Osei: In private, you can have fewer tenants, but we still keep it bounded. It’s typically per data class and per store/region, not per request. You can optionally tag by tenant if you have multi-tenant in your deployment, but default is low-cardinality.

[07:14] Miguel Santos: What about backlog scenarios? Like we had this last year with another system, maintenance window and then deletion jobs fell behind for a week.

[07:24] Vivek Kulkarni: That’s expected occasionally. There are knobs to throttle and to catch up. The dashboards show backlog size, like “records eligible for deletion” or time lag. And we have runbooks: if you’re behind, you can temporarily increase purge throughput, then revert.

[07:42] Erin Wallace: But if we’re behind, doesn’t that violate retention policy? Like we promised 30 days, but now it’s 37.

[07:49] Marcus Lin: In compliance terms, you want to be careful with wording. It’s “configured retention with best-effort enforcement,” but we’re trying to make it measurable. For regulated customers we typically set alert thresholds so you’ll know before it drifts materially.

[08:05] Priya Desai: For our auditors, we need to show controls, not perfection. Like: policy exists, it is enforced, deviations are detected and remediated.

[08:13] Markus Klein: Exactly. That maps to what we include in the compliance reporting pack: retention config export plus evidence that purge jobs are running and not failing.

[08:22] Erin Wallace: Ok, talk about “legal hold.” If we have an investigation, we might need to preserve logs longer. But our retention policy says delete at 30 days.

[08:33] Marcus Lin: So we have a legal hold / incident hold workflow. The short version: an authorized admin can apply a hold for a defined scope and time window, and that hold is itself an audited event. While hold is active, purge jobs skip deletion for that scope.

[08:50] Erin Wallace: Who is “authorized admin”? Like do we define that via RBAC?

[08:54] Marcus Lin: Yes. It’s tied to roles. In many customers we recommend a break-glass role that’s tightly limited. The key is: holds should be exceptional and visible.

[09:06] Miguel Santos: Is the hold per data class? Like can we hold audit logs but still delete request logs?

[09:11] Kevin Osei: Yes, holds are per data class and can be narrower, depending on what you configure. The policy schema allows exceptions, but we keep it constrained so it’s understandable.

[09:24] Hannah Cho: Where does the hold state live? In the policy service?

[09:28] Kevin Osei: Correct. It’s part of retention policy state, with change history.

[09:34] Priya Desai: “Change history” is important. We need a record of when retention changed and who approved.

[09:40] Kevin Osei: Yes. Retention changes generate audit log entries and are visible in change history. In the export, you can include “current policy” plus “policy change log.”

[09:55] Markus Klein: Erin, do you want to go deeper on the “where logs live” question? I feel like we answered abstractly, but maybe you need specifics for your security review doc.

[10:04] Erin Wallace: Yeah. Specifically: in private, is there any central Redwood service that receives audit logs? Or are audit logs also local.

[10:11] Vivek Kulkarni: Audit logs are local. The audit log store is inside your environment. There is an exporter service that can package them for you, but the data doesn’t go to Redwood unless you push it.

[10:24] Erin Wallace: Exporter packages them—like as a file?

[10:27] Kevin Osei: Yes. Think of it as: you request an export for a time window, optionally filtered by actor or event type, and it produces a JSON and/or CSV. For the compliance pack, we also can attach the retention config export in the same bundle.

[10:45] Priya Desai: And the “compliance reporting pack” is a bundle of multiple things?

[10:49] Markus Klein: Yes. Let’s switch to that. The baseline pack includes: (1) audit-log coverage summary—basically which event types are emitted; (2) retention configuration export; (3) data residency / region summary; (4) access control / RBAC report; and (5) an evidence checklist aligned to SOC 2 / ISO style controls.

[11:12] Priya Desai: Does it produce a PDF? Auditors always ask for PDF even if they end up using the CSV.

[11:18] Kevin Osei: We can render a PDF “cover” or summary, but the ground truth is JSON/CSV. We’ve been versioning the template, so you’ll get “pack v1.0” with stable fields.

[11:32] Erin Wallace: How do you get data residency summary in private? It’s our VPC, so isn’t that obvious?

[11:37] Vivek Kulkarni: It’s obvious to engineers, but the report includes: which region(s) the deployment is configured for, whether any cross-region failover is enabled, where the object storage buckets are, and KMS key IDs (not the secrets), stuff like that. It’s basically an attestation of configuration.

[11:56] Miguel Santos: And RBAC report, what does that contain?

[11:59] Marcus Lin: It’s a list of roles and permissions and which principals have them—users, service accounts. Also SSO/SAML config status if you’re using it.

[12:10] Hannah Cho: Can we integrate audit logs with our SIEM instead of pulling quarterly packs?

[12:16] Kevin Osei: Yes. The exporter supports streaming to a destination in your environment—like your SIEM collector—depending on how you set it up. But the baseline compliance pack is “generate on demand,” often quarterly or during security review.

[12:33] Erin Wallace: One worry: audit event completeness. We had a vendor where certain event types were missing, like permission changes.

[12:41] Marcus Lin: We track an “audit log coverage” matrix. It enumerates what we consider “must have” event types: authentication events, authorization changes, retention policy changes, report exports, key management events, admin actions. The compliance pack includes that list and which are enabled.

[12:59] Priya Desai: Is it possible some are not enabled?

[13:02] Kevin Osei: In private, you can configure verbosity, but for critical security events we treat them as always on. Some optional events might be toggled.

[13:13] Miguel Santos: Let’s go back to purge. How does purge work for object storage? If request logs are in S3, can we use lifecycle policies instead of a job?

[13:24] Vivek Kulkarni: Yes. In fact, we recommend that for big volume logs. The “retention policy service” can generate recommended lifecycle rules, or the installer can apply them if you want. Then “verification” becomes: verify lifecycle rules are present and that objects older than TTL are expiring.

[13:45] Hannah Cho: But lifecycle expiration is not immediate sometimes. It’s like… Amazon does it within a day.

[13:50] Vivek Kulkarni: Exactly. So we document purge semantics: TTL is in days, deletion is “within the next purge cycle / lifecycle window.” That’s why dashboards track lag.

[14:03] Erin Wallace: Ok. For database-backed stores, what is the store? Like are you using Postgres for logs?

[14:09] Vivek Kulkarni: Not for high-volume request logs. Those can be object storage plus optionally OpenSearch. Audit logs are much smaller and can be in a relational store or a log index, depending on the deployment. We’ll map to your preference.

[14:26] Miguel Santos: We run ClickHouse for logs internally. Can you write there?

[14:31] Vivek Kulkarni: It’s possible. We have reference integrations but we’d treat that as an implementation detail. The purge job framework needs to know how to delete by timestamp and how to page. We can work with your infra team.

[14:48] Markus Klein: I’m hearing an action item: we should produce a “data class → storage backend → purge mechanism” table for your exact deployment.

[14:56] Erin Wallace: Yes please. That’s exactly what I need for our internal architecture review.

[15:01] Markus Klein: Cool, we’ll do that.

[15:06] Priya Desai: Can you explain “policy evaluation in control plane” again? Why not just configure each store independently?

[15:13] Kevin Osei: Good question. If you configure every store independently, you lose a unified view and you can’t prove what the effective policy is. With central evaluation, you have one schema: per data class TTL, optional overrides per region, plus exceptions like holds. Then the purge jobs read the evaluated policy.

[15:34] Kevin Osei: Also, changes are audited. If someone changes a lifecycle rule manually, you’d miss it. We at least can detect drift: policy says 30 days but bucket lifecycle says 90, that shows up as drift.

[15:50] Hannah Cho: Drift detection is really good. We’ve been burned by “config sprawl.”

[15:54] Erin Wallace: If we have multiple regions—say us-west and us-east—can we set different TTLs? Some of our east region is for DR and we’d rather keep less.

[16:05] Kevin Osei: The schema supports per-region overrides, yes. But we put guardrails on it because it can get confusing.

[16:13] Priya Desai: And do those overrides show in the compliance report pack?

[16:17] Kevin Osei: Yes. The retention export includes the resolved policy by region.

[16:22] Markus Klein: Quick check: are you expecting single region only, or multi-region?

[16:27] Miguel Santos: Initially single region. But compliance is asking about DR. So we need an answer for both.

[16:35] Vivek Kulkarni: For Private, DR patterns vary. Some customers keep compute in one region and replicate only artifacts, not logs. We can design it so logs aren’t replicated if that’s your policy.

[16:50] Erin Wallace: That would be preferred. Prompts should not be replicated.

[16:54] Marcus Lin: And again, prompts shouldn’t be stored at all in the platform unless you enable it. But yes, if you use any payload logging, you want to treat that as sensitive.

[17:09] Miguel Santos: What about traces? Tracing sometimes includes request attributes.

[17:14] Marcus Lin: Great callout. Tracing needs to be configured to avoid capturing payload. We recommend limiting trace attributes to request IDs and performance metrics. The retention controls include traces/metrics as a data class, but you still need “what do we collect.”

[17:31] Hannah Cho: So retention controls is not a substitute for logging standards.

[17:35] Marcus Lin: Exactly. It’s about lifecycle. Collection and redaction is separate, but we can provide guidance.

[17:45] Markus Klein: Let’s look at the compliance pack delivery. Priya, do you need an automated scheduled generation, or manual is ok?

[17:53] Priya Desai: Manual is ok if it’s predictable. Like a button that says “generate pack for Q1” and then we save it.

[18:02] Kevin Osei: That’s the MVP: generate on demand, time-windowed. You can do “last 90 days” or explicit dates. It bundles exports and a checklist.

[18:16] Erin Wallace: Where is that generated? In the same cluster? Or is it a Redwood SaaS service.

[18:21] Vivek Kulkarni: In private, it runs in your environment. Think of it as a generator service that reads from local stores and writes a package to your object storage.

[18:32] Miguel Santos: And access controlled? Like only compliance role can generate.

[18:36] Marcus Lin: Yes. There is RBAC around “export audit logs” and “generate compliance pack.” Exports themselves are audited.

[18:48] Priya Desai: That helps. We also need to show that access to logs is restricted.

[18:54] Marcus Lin: That’s part of the pack: RBAC report and evidence checklist.

[19:04] Erin Wallace: Let’s drill into “purge semantics.” If TTL is 30 days, does that mean record is deleted exactly at day 30? Or could it be “within X days.”

[19:16] Kevin Osei: It’s not to the minute. It’s best described as: items older than TTL are eligible for deletion, and deletion happens on the next purge cycle. Purge cycle frequency is configurable—daily is common. For object lifecycle, the cloud provider may take up to 24-48 hours.

[19:34] Erin Wallace: Ok. We should document that because legal asks.

[19:37] Markus Klein: Agreed. We’ll include that in the architecture write-up.

[19:44] Miguel Santos: How do you handle “disabled logging” vs “TTL = 0”? Some systems interpret TTL 0 as delete everything, which is scary.

[19:52] Kevin Osei: Yeah, we explicitly avoid TTL = 0 semantics. Disabled is a separate flag. TTL has min/max validation. So you won’t accidentally set “0” and wipe everything.

[20:06] Hannah Cho: Can you also prevent someone from setting retention too long? Like we have policy caps.

[20:11] Kevin Osei: Yes. There are max TTL constraints by tier. In private, you can configure allowed ranges, but we still want guardrails.

[20:22] Priya Desai: That’s good for demonstrating governance.

[20:27] Erin Wallace: Does the purge job ever delete audit logs? That’s a sensitive topic. Some auditors want audit logs to be immutable.

[20:36] Marcus Lin: Audit logs can have retention too, but “immutability” is a separate control. In private, you can store audit logs in an append-only store or push to a WORM bucket or your SIEM. The platform can help export, but immutability is generally handled by your storage policy.

[20:57] Hannah Cho: We can do S3 Object Lock in compliance mode.

[21:00] Vivek Kulkarni: Exactly. And then retention becomes “we stop writing after TTL”? Not quite. You would still write events, but deletion is prevented by object lock until it expires.

[21:14] Erin Wallace: If object lock prevents deletion, doesn’t that conflict with our retention policy?

[21:19] Priya Desai: Actually for audit logs, our policy is like 7 years, so it’s fine.

[21:24] Marcus Lin: Right. The retention policy should match the immutability. The compliance pack can reflect that: “audit logs stored in WORM bucket with retention X.”

[21:39] Miguel Santos: Switching topics: “artifacts” like eval datasets. We might want to run prompt evals. Are those stored?

[21:47] Kevin Osei: In private, if you upload eval datasets to the console, they live in your object storage. Retention controls apply if you want, but usually those are treated as artifacts with longer retention. Also, you can keep them in git and not upload.

[22:05] Erin Wallace: Ok. Another thing: request IDs. If we don’t log prompts, can we still correlate from application logs to Redwood inference?

[22:14] Vivek Kulkarni: Yes, we propagate request IDs, and you can log those on your side. The gateway emits metadata logs with request IDs, model ID, latency, and errors.

[22:27] Miguel Santos: Good. That’s essential.

[22:31] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick walk-through of what a compliance pack might look like. Kevin, can you outline the sections in order?

[22:39] Kevin Osei: Sure. The pack typically has: a manifest file with pack version and generation timestamp; a retention_policy.json export; an audit_log_export.json (or csv) for the requested time window; an “audit coverage” summary—like a table of event types; a “data residency” summary; an “access controls” report; and then a checklist doc with links: “screenshot of retention settings page,” “evidence of purge job dashboards,” etc.

[23:10] Priya Desai: The checklist is internal only or customer-facing?

[23:14] Kevin Osei: Both. We can provide an internal one and a customer-ready version. The customer-ready one avoids internal URLs.

[23:24] Erin Wallace: Do you have a concept of “download pack from console”? Or is it CLI.

[23:29] Vivek Kulkarni: For private, it can be in the console UI, if you deploy the console. Otherwise you can trigger via API/CLI. The artifact ends up in your bucket.

[23:45] Hannah Cho: Our compliance team will prefer UI. Engineers can use CLI.

[23:49] Markus Klein: Noted.

[23:52] Miguel Santos: I want to understand what events are in audit logs. Is it like every request? That would be huge.

[24:00] Marcus Lin: No. Audit logs are admin/security events. Not per inference request. Request logs are separate.

[24:10] Miguel Santos: Ok, good.

[24:12] Erin Wallace: Are retention policy changes themselves in audit logs.

[24:16] Marcus Lin: Yes, that’s one of the key event types.

[24:22] Priya Desai: Can we filter exports to “policy changes only” for a period?

[24:27] Kevin Osei: Yes. The exporter supports event_type filters. Like “RETENTION_POLICY_UPDATED” or “ROLE_GRANTED.”

[24:39] Erin Wallace: How stable are those event type strings? We don’t want to build something that breaks.

[24:45] Kevin Osei: We version the schema. Event types are treated as stable, and additions are backward compatible. If we ever deprecate, we’d map.

[24:58] Hannah Cho: Ok.

[25:00] Markus Klein: I’m going to time check—we’re at about 25 minutes. We can spend the next 20 on purge mechanics and verification, then do recap.

[25:08] Erin Wallace: Sounds good. Verification: you mentioned dashboards. Are those included by default in private?

[25:14] Vivek Kulkarni: Yes, part of the observability pack. You’ll get dashboards for TTL lag, purge errors, and backlog. Alerts are recommended, with thresholds you can adjust.

[25:29] Miguel Santos: What are typical thresholds?

[25:32] Vivek Kulkarni: Example: if ttl_lag_seconds exceeds 2 days for request logs, page; for audit logs maybe 7 days depending on retention. Purge failures > 0 sustained over 15 minutes triggers warning. We’ll tune with you.

[25:51] Hannah Cho: Do purge jobs have concurrency controls? We had a job that locked tables.

[25:57] Kevin Osei: Yes. They run with safety limits: max rows per batch, max runtime per cycle, and pause between batches. And you can run in “dry-run” mode to estimate impact.

[26:15] Erin Wallace: Dry-run is great.

[26:18] Miguel Santos: How do you handle “backfills”? Like if we turn on retention controls after we already have 6 months of logs.

[26:26] Kevin Osei: First run will see a lot of eligible records. We ramp gradually. There’s a “backfill mode” to catch up without overloading. Metrics show progress.

[26:43] Priya Desai: Would auditors care that it takes a week to backfill?

[26:47] Marcus Lin: Usually not, as long as you document the rollout and show the control is now in place. Also you can do a one-time manual purge if needed.

[26:59] Erin Wallace: Another angle: if we have an incident, can on-call extend retention temporarily for debugging? That can conflict with policy.

[27:09] Marcus Lin: That’s where break-glass comes in. But we recommend you don’t shorten retention too aggressively if it harms operations. Many customers do request metadata logs for 14-30 days, not 1 day.

[27:25] Miguel Santos: Yeah, we’re thinking 30 days for metadata, 0 for payload.

[27:30] Erin Wallace: We might do 7 days for metadata, but we’ll see.

[27:34] Vivek Kulkarni: We can help you pick defaults. In private, our secure defaults are “payload logging off,” request metadata logs on with moderate TTL, audit logs longer.

[27:49] Priya Desai: We should align on “safe defaults” because we’ll get asked.

[27:54] Markus Klein: Totally.

[27:57] Erin Wallace: One more: does Redwood store anything in the control plane that could contain customer data? Like retention configs maybe include tenant IDs.

[28:08] Vivek Kulkarni: In private, control plane is in your environment as well, so it stores config in your environment. If you choose a hybrid model, it would store configuration metadata, not payloads. But for your use case we’ve been discussing fully private.

[28:25] Erin Wallace: Ok.

[28:27] Miguel Santos: When you say “policy evaluation cache,” does that mean requests might keep using old policy?

[28:34] Kevin Osei: Purge jobs read policy periodically, and there’s a cache to avoid hammering config DB, but it’s invalidated on change. Worst case, you have a short window (minutes) where the next purge cycle uses the previous value. We document it.

[28:54] Hannah Cho: That’s acceptable.

[28:57] Priya Desai: We also need a record of “policy effective time.”

[29:02] Kevin Osei: Yes—policy changes have timestamps and audit events.
